eolithic.e: From French éolithique; from Ancient Greek Ἠώς (Ēṓs, “dawn”) + λίθος (líthos, “stone”) + -ic. By surface analysis, eo- + lith- + -ic.

d.g: Alternative spelling of aeolotropic.
Of or pertaining to an eon
eon-long, everlasting

eonian.e: From Ancient Greek αἰώνιος (aiṓnios, “lasting for an age; perpetual; eternal”) + -an, the former from αἰών (aiṓn, “lifetime; aeon; age; generation”) (whence also eon, aeon) + -ιος (-ios, adjective suffix).

d.g: That is readily stained with eosin.
Of, pertaining to an eosinophil or to eosinophilia.

eosinophilic.e: English eosin Ancient Greek -ο- (-o-)der. Latin -o-bor. English -o- English -philic English eosinophilic From eosin + -o- + -philic.

d.g: from 58 million to 40 million years ago;  presence of modern mammals
An extinct early Eocene mammal (Hyracotherium leporinum), ancestral to the modern horse.

eohippus.e: Originally a genus name, Eohippus, formed in New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἠώς (ēṓs, “dawn”) + ἵππος (híppos, “horse”). By surface analysis, eo- + Latin hippus.

d.g: Alternative spelling of aeolian.
Of the wind; referring to the action or the power of wind.

eolic.e: From Latin Aeolicus, from Ancient Greek Αἴολος (Aíolos, “Aeolus, god of the winds”).

d.g: Crudely chopped flints, believed to be naturally produced by geological processes such as glaciation.
Eternity, the duration of the universe.
An immeasurably or indefinitely long period of time.
A long period of time.

d.g: A period of one billion (short scale, i.e. 1,000,000,000) years; a gigayear.

eon.e: From Latin aeon, from Ancient Greek αἰών (aiṓn, “age, era”).

d.g: a theropod dinosaur of the genus Eoraptor

A red, acidic dye commonly used in histological stains.
d.x: The hematoxylin and eosin stain (H&E) is the most widely used histological stain.

eosin.e: Borrowed from German Eosin, coined by Heinrich Caro, from Ancient Greek ἠώς (ēṓs, “dawn”) + -in.

d.g: A form of agranulocytosis where the number of eosinophil granulocytes is lower than expected.
A white blood cell responsible for combating infection by parasites in the body.
Alternative form of eosinophilic.

eosinophil.e: From German eosinophil, from eosin (“rose dye, from Ancient Greek ἠώς (ēṓs, “dawn”) + -in”) + -o- + -phil.

d.g: Alternative form of eosinophil.
The condition of having a high concentration of eosinophils (eosinophil granulocytes) in the blood.

eosinophilia.e: Coined 1879 by American biologist Paul Ehrlich from eosin (“rosy, dawn-colored”) + -o- + -philia. By surface analysis, eosinophil + -ia.
